messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 74

Mr. Tran, a 75-year-old widowed man of South Eastern Asian descent, has lived through many challenges throughout his life, but the trauma of his son’s near-fatal illness continues to haunt him daily. As a former cybersecurity analyst, Mr. Tran once prided himself on his ability to anticipate and mitigate risks, yet he found himself utterly powerless during that harrowing time. It was nearly two decades ago when his youngest son fell severely ill with a life-threatening condition. The diagnosis came as a shock; the young man had always been robust and healthy. For weeks, Mr. Tran visited the hospital daily, watching helplessly as his son fought for his life in intensive care. Despite numerous medical interventions, there were moments when he feared he would lose him forever. Those days seemed to blur into an endless loop of uncertainty and dread. Since that time, Mr. Tran has struggled with intrusive thoughts and memories of those painful weeks. He often wakes up in the middle of the night, drenched in sweat, reliving the sight of his son’s pale face attached to tubes and monitors. These nightmares are so vivid that he feels as if he is back in the hospital again, helpless and unable to protect his child. Mr. Tran's anxiety has also spilled into his waking hours, making it difficult for him to concentrate on tasks at work. As a cybersecurity analyst, attention to detail is crucial, but lately, he finds himself easily distracted by intrusive thoughts about that time. He tries to immerse himself in the technical aspects of his job—working with complex algorithms and data encryption—but often finds himself reverting back to those haunting memories. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Mr. Tran has developed a routine that revolves around structure and predictability. He meticulously plans every aspect of his day, from the moment he wakes up until he goes to bed at night. This includes setting specific times for work tasks, meals, and even leisure activities. However, despite this meticulous planning, he still feels a constant sense of unease. One of Mr. Tran’s most noticeable symptoms is hyperarousal. Even in calm environments, such as his quiet home or the office, he remains on high alert. The slightest noise—a car door slamming, an unexpected phone call—can trigger a surge of anxiety and panic. He often checks and rechecks his surroundings, feeling as though danger could lurk around any corner. Mr. Tran’s relationship with his son has been strained since that time due to the emotional toll it took on both of them. The younger man, now in his late 30s, is well aware of his father's struggles but sometimes feels like he cannot bridge the gap between them. Mr. Tran frequently isolates himself from family gatherings and social events, preferring to stay home where he can maintain a sense of control over his environment. Despite these challenges, Mr. Tran remains deeply committed to his work as a cybersecurity analyst. His expertise is valued by his colleagues, but he often feels that the job has become more about fulfilling an obligation than finding fulfillment. He acknowledges that his condition affects his performance and interacts with clients less frequently than before, preferring to handle tasks remotely. Mr. Tran's life revolves around managing these constant reminders of the trauma he experienced. Each day is a battle between his past and present, as he navigates through work and daily routines while grappling with vivid memories of those harrowing weeks. His resilience is evident in his ability to function despite the persistent symptoms that continue to affect his daily life. In moments of quiet reflection, Mr. Tran wonders if he will ever be free from these haunting memories. He sometimes feels like a stranger trapped within his own mind, struggling to reconcile the trauma with the present reality. Despite the challenges, he continues to find small pockets of solace in routine and familiar activities, hoping that one day the pain might lessen enough for him to reclaim some sense of peace.
